newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TNT sees higher profits and success for KPN.
newsitem.headline: TNT sees higher profits and success for KPN.

text.p: Australian-based international transport firm TNT Ltd said on Wednesday it expected higher first half profits and forecast that its A$2 billion (US$1.6 billion) takeover by Dutch postal and telecoms group Koninklijke PTT Nederland (KPN) would soon get European regulatory approval.

TNT chairman Fred Millar told the company's annual meeting he expected approval from the European Commission in the next week or so, describing this as one of the final hurdles for KPN before its friendly bid closes on November 19.
"If they (the EC) indicate they want more time they are allowed to take an extra four months," Millar told reporters after the annual meeting of shareholders.

"We have no indication that they are going to seek an extra period," he said, noting there was some concern about the competitive implications by other Dutch courier and freight express firms. Australian regulators have approved the takeover.

Millar said TNT had increased operating profit in the first three months of 1996/97 by 14.7 percent to A$27.0 million, thanks in large part to the earlier sale of the half share in underperforming regional carrier Ansett Airways.

TNT's other Australian operations remained a disappointment, with some of these assets tipped by industry analysts as likely to be sold by KPN, which was attracted to TNT's European express freight and logistics divisions.

TNT managing director David Mortimer, who plans to join KPN as a regional executive, said first half profits were also expected to rise with a substantial contribution from interest income on the A$325 million paid by Air New Zealand for the Ansett stake.
"A big factor in the TNT results last year was Ansett. It is no longer of the operation, so the decoupling of those equity accounted losses has a significant positive effect," he said.
Millar, referring to other potential hurdles for KPN, said a rival bidder had not emerged and no discussions had been held with Bankers Trust which holds a 19.99 percent blocking stake.

KPN, which has 19.8 percent of TNT from shareholder acceptances and on-market purchases by its broker County Natwest, bid A$2.45 per share for TNT on October 2. The Dutch company's bid is based on winning at least 90 percent control.

The KPN offer was more than 50 percent above TNT's previous closing level but BT acquired shares just below the bid price, saying this was a good deal for KPN which wanted the synergies from the European GD Express Worldwide freight joint venture.
The BT purchase also led to speculation the investment bank might seek a rival bidder such as Federal Express Corp of the United States which wanted to expand its European operations.
Analysts said it was now unlikely that a rival bid would be made and that BT was expected to sell its holding to KPN just before the closed.

"It has been mooted that DHL, FedEx, or UPS will make a higher offer but the only glitch with that issue is that they would probably want to buy GD Express," said an analyst with a London-based brokerage firm.
"And the poison pill in the prospectus that KPN can buy it for A$284 million basically removed an asset that they would want," the analyst said.
